Bamah
BAH-mah
n. (the name Ezekiel gives to the high place of Israel's idolatry; named once)
Hebrew bamah, a high place or elevation; the ordinary word for the hill-shrines of Canaanite and apostate Israelite worship, used once at Ezekiel 20:29 as a proper name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

Bamah is the common Hebrew noun for a high place, turned into a name by way of rebuke: “Then I said unto them, What is the high place whereunto ye go? And the name thereof is called Bamah unto this day” (Ezekiel 20:29). The question is contemptuous. God has been reciting the history of Israel's rebellions, and when He reaches the shrines on the hills He asks what the thing even is, and then says that its name is simply High Place — as if to say the whole apparatus has no more content than the hill it stands on. The charge immediately before explains it: “For when I had brought them into the land, for the which I lifted up mine hand to give it to them, then they saw every high hill, and all the thick trees, and they offered there their sacrifices” (Ezekiel 20:28). The sin is not that they stopped sacrificing but that they chose their own places to do it. The law had promised the end of these shrines from the beginning: “And I will destroy your high places, and cut down your images, and cast your carcases upon the carcases of your idols, and my soul shall abhor you” (Leviticus 26:30), and the faithful kings carried it out: “He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves” (2 Kings 18:4). Bamah is the name of will-worship exposed by being named plainly.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Bamah is the Hebrew word for a high place, used once as a proper name at Ezekiel 20:29.

expand to see more

Bamah is Hebrew bamah, a high place or elevation.

It is the standing word for the hill-shrines of idolatrous worship.

It occurs once as a proper name, at Ezekiel 20:29.

The name is given in rebuke, as though the shrine had no other content.

The high places were marked for destruction in the law, Leviticus 26:30.

Key Scripture

Eze 20:29 — "Then I said unto them, What is the high place whereunto ye go? And the name thereof is called Bamah unto this day."

Eze 20:28 — "For when I had brought them into the land, for the which I lifted up mine hand to give it to them, then they saw every high hill, and all the thick trees, and they offered there their sacrifices, and there they presented the provocation of their offering: there also they made their sweet savour, and poured out there their drink offerings."

Lev 26:30 — "And I will destroy your high places, and cut down your images, and cast your carcases upon the carcases of your idols, and my soul shall abhor you."

2Ki 18:4 — "He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan."

Modern Corruption

The high places are excused as sincere local devotion to the true God, where Scripture names them as self-chosen worship and condemns them as such.

expand to see more

A familiar reading makes the high places a harmless folk piety: the people meant to worship the LORD, only nearer home, and the prophets were severe about a matter of arrangement. Ezekiel 20 answers that the arrangement was the sin. They saw every high hill and the thick trees and offered there (Ezekiel 20:28) — the choice was made by the eye, and the worship followed the scenery. Worship that God has not commanded is not a lesser obedience; it is will-worship, and the Scripture treats it as provocation, not as enthusiasm needing better direction.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the regulative principle: what God commands in His worship is required, and what He has not commanded is not permitted. Bamah is what a self-chosen shrine is called when God names it, and the name is a bare noun, because there was nothing else in it to name.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bamah, a high place; used as a name at Ezekiel 20:29.

expand to see more

Hebrew bamah, a high place or elevation.

The ordinary term for a hill-shrine of idolatrous worship.

Made a proper name once, at Ezekiel 20:29.

The plural bamoth lies behind many Authorized Version place-names.

Marked for destruction in the law and removed by the faithful kings.
